topics.title: AI-Native Applications
topics.description: AI-native applications are products where generative models power the core user experience, from code editors and voice agents to customer support and media generation. Each category has different inference requirements. Agents generate many inference calls per user action; chat applications prioritize TTFT; voice applications need low end-to-end latency for natural conversation.
resources: Open the AI Product Builder roadmap
How to Build an AI-Native Services Company

topics.title: NVIDIA GenAI-Perf
topics.description: GenAI-Perf is NVIDIA's inference benchmarking tool, designed to work across TensorRT-LLM, Triton Inference Server, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints. It generates synthetic workloads with configurable sequence length distributions and concurrency levels and outputs standard latency and throughput metrics including TTFT, ITL, and TPS percentiles.

topics.title: Arithmetic Intensity
topics.description: Arithmetic intensity is a property of an algorithm: the number of floating-point operations performed per byte of memory read or written. A large matrix multiplication has high arithmetic intensity because the same weights participate in many operations per load; a decode forward pass has low arithmetic intensity because each weight is loaded from VRAM and used once per token. Comparing a workload's arithmetic intensity against the GPU's ops:byte ratio is the fastest way to diagnose whether adding compute or adding bandwidth would help.
resources: A guide to LLM inference and performance
Arithmetic Intensity : Understand Op limits — Memory or Compute
Arithmetic Intensity Explained: The Formula and Why It Predicts GPU Speedup
Compute-Bound or Memory-Bound? Arithmetic Intensity Explained

topics.title: Asynchronous Inference
topics.description: Asynchronous inference is a fire-and-forget request model where the client submits a job, receives an immediate acknowledgment, and retrieves the result later via a webhook. It is suited for throughput-sensitive, latency-insensitive workloads like bulk document embedding or corpus transcription. Async jobs have much longer time limits than synchronous requests and require robust server-side queuing.

topics.title: Asynchronous Inference
topics.description: Asynchronous inference is a fire-and-forget request model where the client submits a job, receives an immediate acknowledgment, and retrieves the result later via a webhook. It is suited for throughput-sensitive, latency-insensitive workloads like bulk document embedding or corpus transcription. Async jobs have much longer time limits than synchronous requests and require robust server-side queuing.

topics.title: Attention Mechanism
topics.description: Attention is the mechanism transformers use to relate each token to all previous tokens via query, key, and value projections. During decode, each new token attends to every prior token, and the KV cache stores precomputed keys and values to avoid recomputation. Attention is the most expensive and most heavily optimized operation in LLM inference.

topics.title: Attention Optimization
topics.description: Attention optimization refers to techniques designed to improve the computational efficiency and memory usage of the attention mechanism within transformer models. Because standard attention scales quadratically with input sequence length, these optimizations aim to reduce computation and memory overhead. By streamlining how tokens interact with one another, these methods allow models to process longer inputs faster and run on hardware with less available memory.
resources: Advanced Attention Mechanisms in Transformer LLMs
​Sequential Attention: Making AI models leaner and faster without sacrificing accuracy

topics.title: Attention Variants
topics.description: Newer attention algorithms reduce the quadratic time complexity of standard attention. Sliding window attention limits each token to attending to the nearest w tokens, turning O(N²) into O(Nw). Linear attention approximates the softmax with a linear-time kernel. Compressed attention periodically compresses earlier context. These variants trade off some quality for better scaling on long sequences.
resources: Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases Enables Input Length Extrapolation
Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces

topics.title: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR)
topics.description: ASR models like Whisper take audio input and produce text transcripts. Whisper is an encoder-decoder model where the decoder, an autoregressive transformer, dominates inference time. TensorRT-LLM with in-flight batching for the decoder delivers the best performance. For real-time transcription, streaming via WebSockets with VAD-segmented chunks achieves round-trip targets of around 200 milliseconds per chunk on optimized deployments.
resources: OpenAI Whisper Models on Hugging Face
What is Automatic Speech Recognition? A Comprehensive Overview of ASR Technology
How streaming ASR inference differs from LLM serving

topics.title: Autoscaling
topics.description: Autoscaling dynamically adjusts the number of active model replicas to match incoming traffic, maintaining latency SLAs while minimizing idle GPU spend. Kubernetes is the standard orchestration layer, scaling replicas within a cluster based on traffic signals and utilization metrics. Key configuration parameters are min replicas, max replicas, the autoscaling window, the scale-down delay, and the concurrency target per replica.
resources: Best practices for autoscaling large language model (LLM) inference workloads
Autoscaling your AI agent under load

topics.title: Benchmarking and Profiling
topics.description: Benchmarking and profiling are how inference engineers turn intuition into evidence. Benchmarking measures system-level throughput and latency under load; profiling zooms in to identify which specific operations are consuming time. Both are prerequisites for making optimization decisions with confidence.
resources: Benchmarking AI Inference Providers: How to Compare Performance Fairly
Benchmarking AI inference on CPUs: A transparent blueprint for the enterprise

topics.title: BERT-style Models
topics.description: BERT-style encoder-only models are the traditional architecture for text embeddings, producing a fixed-size vector by pooling the final hidden states of a bidirectional transformer. They are compact, fast, and well-suited for high-throughput indexing workloads where embedding quality is sufficient for the task. Models like BGE-small and all-MiniLM run efficiently on CPU or fractional GPU instances, making them the lowest-cost embedding option.
resources: Using Sentence Transformers at Hugging Face
BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
Sentence-BERT: Sentence Embeddings using Siamese BERT-Networks

topics.title: Blackwell
topics.description: The Blackwell architecture, released in late 2024 with the B200 and B300, added FP4 Tensor Cores and new microscaling number formats including MXFP8, MXFP4, and NVFP4. B200 GPUs offer approximately 5 petaFLOPS of FP8 compute and up to 8 TB/s of memory bandwidth. They are the current gold standard for demanding inference workloads including large LLMs and video generation.
resources: NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs: Architecture, Features, Specs

topics.title: Bottleneck Analysis
topics.description: Bottleneck analysis identifies whether a given inference workload is limited by compute or by memory bandwidth, which determines which optimizations will actually improve performance. The core tool is the ops:byte ratio: comparing a GPU's peak FLOPS against its peak memory bandwidth reveals the hardware's balance point, and comparing a model operation's arithmetic intensity against that balance point reveals whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound. LLM prefill and image generation are compute-bound; LLM decode is memory-bound.
resources: The Next AI Bottleneck Isn’t the Model: It’s the Inference System
Performance Analysis and Bottleneck Identification in AI Workflows
Distributed AI Inference: Why Placement Is the New Bottleneck

topics.title: Cache-Aware Routing
topics.description: In deployments with multiple replicas, cache-aware routing directs requests to the replica most likely to have a matching prefix already in its KV cache. Without this, a user in a long conversation may hit different replicas each turn, getting cache misses that increase latency. A global KV cache stored on networked SSD allows all replicas to eventually access any cached sequence.
resources: Why Agentic Inference Needs Prefix-Aware Routing Infrastructure
Enabling inference at massive scale with hybrid storage for KV cache offloading.

topics.title: Caching Approaches
topics.description: KV cache reuse is the primary caching strategy in LLM inference, covering both prefix caching (reusing cached KV values across requests that share a common prefix) and KV cache offloading (moving less-used cache blocks to slower storage tiers to free GPU VRAM). A related concern is cache-aware routing, which directs requests to replicas most likely to already hold the relevant cached prefix.
resources: What is Prompt Caching? Optimize LLM Latency with AI Transformers
How KV Cache Speeds Up LLMs for Faster AI Models on GPUs

topics.title: Caching
topics.description: Caching reuses previously computed KV values to avoid redundant prefill computation across requests that share common context. It is one of the most impactful techniques for reducing TTFT in workloads with long system prompts or multi-turn conversations. This group covers the approaches, storage tiers, routing implications, and long-context strategies that make caching effective at scale.
resources: KV Caching Explained: Optimizing Transformer Inference Efficiency
KV Caching in LLMs: A Guide for Developers
KV Cache: The Trick That Makes LLMs Faster
The KV Cache: Memory Usage in Transformers

topics.title: Capacity Management
topics.description: Multi-cloud inference pools GPU capacity from multiple cloud providers and regions into a single schedulable resource, treating distinct compute pools as fungible. This requires a global control plane for deployment and scaling decisions alongside per-cluster workload planes that serve traffic and report utilization. True multi-cloud unlocks greater total capacity, improved reliability through redundancy, lower latency via geographic proximity, and data sovereignty compliance.
resources: How we built Multi-cloud Capacity Management (MCM)

topics.title: Client Integration
topics.description: The client layer connects application code to the inference service and contributes its own slice of end-to-end latency. This group covers the connection overhead, async request patterns, and protocol choices that determine how efficiently client and server communicate.

topics.title: Client Latency Overhead
topics.description: Establishing a new connection between a client and inference server takes tens of milliseconds for TLS handshake, which can represent ten percent or more of a tight latency budget. Session reuse across requests eliminates this overhead for returning clients. Standard SDKs like the OpenAI SDK handle session reuse automatically; custom clients must implement it explicitly.

topics.title: Cold Starts
topics.description: A cold start is the time from zero replicas to serving the first request, including GPU provisioning, container image loading, model weight loading, and inference engine startup or compilation. Reducing cold start time is essential for autoscaling systems to scale down confidently and scale up responsively. Key techniques include quantized weights, local weight caching near the GPU instances, and caching compiled inference engines to disk.
resources: Autoscaling for LLM Inference Serving and Cold Starts
GPU Cold Start on Serverless LLM Inference: 4 Fixes That Actually Work (2026)

topics.title: Compute
topics.description: A GPU's compute capability is determined by its Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs), each containing CUDA Cores for general arithmetic and Tensor Cores for matrix multiply-accumulate operations. Tensor Cores are the primary resource for inference, executing the matmuls that make up the majority of forward pass computation. GPU compute is measured in peak Tensor Core FLOPS at a given precision, and roughly doubles with each new NVIDIA architecture generation.
resources: Understanding GPU Architecture: Structure, Layers, and Performance Explained
What Is GPU Computing and How Does It Work? A Complete Guide
Understanding NVIDIA GPU Hardware as a CUDA C Programmer

topics.title: Constrained Decoding
topics.description: Constrained decoding is the mechanism that enforces structured outputs at the token level. At each sampling step, logits for tokens that would violate the active schema or grammar are masked to zero before sampling, so only valid continuations can be selected. Grammar compilation adds overhead to time to first token, and the interaction with speculative decoding is important to note: some engines disable speculation under hard constraints because draft token acceptance rates drop sharply when only a narrow set of tokens is valid at each step. .
resources: A Guide to Structured Generation Using Constrained Decoding

topics.title: Consumer vs. B2B Workloads
topics.description: Consumer applications are cost-sensitive and have unpredictable traffic spikes, requiring flexible autoscaling and low marginal cost. Business-to-business applications prioritize uptime and consistent low latency, as they often sit in the critical path of revenue-generating workflows. Compliance requirements, including data residency and regulatory certifications, are more common in enterprise deployments.

topics.title: Containerization
topics.description: Containerization packages an inference service and all its dependencies into a Docker image that runs consistently across environments. Inference containers include the CUDA toolkit, Python packages, the inference engine, and any system libraries like ffmpeg for audio processing. Using a pinned dependency tree prevents breaking changes from affecting running services and ensures reproducible builds.

topics.title: Continuous Batching
topics.description: Continuous batching operates at the token level, swapping requests in and out of the batch as they complete individual tokens rather than waiting for a full batch to finish. This keeps GPU utilization high and minimizes the latency penalty of batching compared to static or dynamic batching. All major inference engines implement continuous batching by default.
resources: Continuous Batching: Optimizing LLM Inference Throughput
Continuous Batching Beats Static and Dynamic by up to 2.91x in vLLM
How to Scale LLM Applications With Continuous Batching!
Continuous Batching - How LLM Servers Keep the GPU Full

topics.title: Cost Estimation
topics.description: Dedicated inference cost depends on batch sizing, traffic patterns, and sequence lengths rather than simply on token count. Comparing dedicated versus API costs requires converting per-token API pricing into total cost over a representative time window and comparing it to GPU-hour costs at the same traffic volume. Total cost of ownership also includes engineering time for building and maintaining the inference system.
resources: The Hidden Economics of LLM Inference
LLM Inference Benchmarking: How Much Does Your LLM Inference Cost?
LLM inference cost: what drives it and how to lower it
LLM Cost Calculation Guide for Enterprise AI Teams in 2026

topics.title: CUDA
topics.description: CUDA is NVIDIA's proprietary platform for programming GPUs, consisting of a kernel language (C++), a driver for hardware management, and a runtime API for launching kernels. Every inference engine, framework, and library in the NVIDIA ecosystem depends on CUDA, including cuBLAS — NVIDIA's optimized implementation of standard linear algebra routines and the default backend for matrix multiplications in most inference pipelines. Understanding CUDA is the foundation for diagnosing performance problems that tools and engines cannot solve automatically.
resources: An Even Easier Introduction to CUDA (Updated)
CUDA Programming Course – High-Performance Computing with GPUs

topics.title: Dependency Management
topics.description: Inference dependency chains are long and fragile due to the tight coupling between CUDA versions, framework versions, and hardware architectures. Pinning exact versions of every dependency prevents unexpected breakage when upstream packages release updates. Containers for newly released models often initially depend on pre-release software builds and need to be rebuilt on stable releases within days of the model launch.

topics.title: Desktop Inference
topics.description: Desktop inference runs on consumer hardware, primarily Apple M-series unified memory systems and high-end NVIDIA consumer GPUs. Apple hardware offers very large unified memory capacity at moderate bandwidth, enabling larger models than discrete consumer GPUs; NVIDIA consumer GPUs offer higher bandwidth with smaller capacity. Tools like Ollama and llama.cpp make it practical to run aggressively quantized models on consumer hardware with minimal setup.
resources: What Is Local AI Inference — and Why It Might Change How You Use AI

topics.title: Diffusion Models
topics.description: Diffusion models generate images by starting from random noise and iteratively denoising it over 30 to 50 steps, guided by a text prompt. Each step runs the denoiser twice, once with conditioning and once without, to apply classifier-free guidance. The entire process operates in a low-dimensional latent space rather than full pixel space to make attention computationally feasible.
resources: Diffusion Models for AI Image Generation
How AI Image Generators Work (Stable Diffusion / DALL-E)

topics.title: Disaggregation
topics.description: Disaggregation separates the prefill and decode phases onto independent GPU instances that can scale separately. The prefill engine processes the input sequence and sends the resulting KV cache to the decode engine via the hardware interconnect. This removes the resource contention between compute-heavy prefill and memory-heavy decode. Disaggregation is most effective at high traffic volumes, for large models, and with prefill-heavy workloads like code editors.
resources: Beyond the Buzz: A Pragmatic Take on Inference Disaggregation
Disaggregated Serving in LLM Inference, Explained
Encoder Disaggregation in vLLM: Scaling Multimodal Serving with EPD
Why Separating Prefill and Decode Makes LLMs Faster | vLLM, LLM-D and NIXL

topics.title: Distillation
topics.description: Distillation trains a smaller student model to emulate a larger teacher model by exposing it to the teacher's probability distributions, not just its final outputs. Unlike fine-tuning on synthetic data, distillation transfers the teacher's reasoning behavior. The resulting student model is smaller and faster while retaining much of the teacher's quality on the same tasks.
resources: How Knowledge Distillation Works and When to Use It
Introduction to model distillation: Efficient knowledge transfer for AI applications
Model Distillation: How to Steal a Billion-Dollar AI

topics.title: Draft-Target Speculative Decoding
topics.description: Draft-target speculation uses a small draft model, typically at least ten times smaller than the target, to generate draft tokens for the target model to verify. The draft model should share the same tokenizer and general behavior as the target, often being a smaller member of the same model family. It is the simplest speculation method to set up but introduces the most overhead due to running a separate model.
resources: Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding
An Introduction to Speculative Decoding for Reducing Latency in AI Inference

topics.title: EAGLE
topics.description: EAGLE is a purpose-built speculation method where a small draft model is trained to accept hidden states from the target model as input. By seeing the target's internal representations, EAGLE achieves higher acceptance rates and longer draft sequences (up to eight tokens) than using a general-purpose small model. It integrates into the same forward pass as the target model, eliminating the orchestration overhead of separate draft and target model runs.
resources: EAGLE: Speculative Sampling Requires Rethinking Feature Uncertainty
EAGLE-2: Faster Inference of Language Models with Dynamic Draft Trees
EAGLE-3: Scaling up Inference Acceleration of Large Language Models via Training-Time Test
EAGLE and EAGLE-2: Lossless Inference Acceleration for LLMs - Hongyang Zhang
Speculative Decoding, Explained: Why EAGLE-3 Finally Scales | 20-Min Deep Dive

topics.title: Embedding Model Inference
topics.description: TensorRT-LLM with its optimized XQA attention kernel offers the best performance for embedding models with LLM backbones. FP8 quantization of weights provides performance gains with minimal quality loss, verified by checking cosine similarity between quantized and original output vectors. Embedding models are small enough that horizontal scaling across individual GPU replicas is more effective than multi-GPU parallelism.
resources: What Actually Makes Embedding Model Inference Fast?

topics.title: Embedding Models
topics.description: Embedding models convert variable-length text or image input into a fixed-length vector that encodes semantic meaning. These vectors are used in RAG, search, recommendation, and agent memory systems. Embedding inference has two distinct traffic profiles: high-throughput backfills for bulk indexing and low-latency lookups for real-time user queries, which are best served by separate deployments.
resources: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
Sentence-BERT: Sentence Embeddings using Siamese BERT-Networks
What Are Embedding Models? Benefits and Best Practices

topics.title: Encoder-Decoder Architectures
topics.description: Neural networks can be organized as encoder-only, decoder-only, or encoder-decoder models. Modern LLMs are decoder-only. Encoder-only models like BERT are used for text embeddings and classification. Encoder-decoder models like Whisper use an encoder to process input into an internal representation and a decoder to generate output tokens autoregressively. Each architecture has different inference characteristics and tooling requirements.

topics.title: End-to-End Metrics
topics.description: End-to-end latency includes inference time, network round-trip, queue time, and client-side overhead. Inference-only metrics tell you how well the model server performs; end-to-end metrics tell you what users actually experience. When inference time is fast but end-to-end time is slow, the bottleneck is in infrastructure or client code, not the GPU.
resources: 10 LLM Inference Metrics Every AI Engineer Must Know
9 Key LLM Inference Metrics Explained in 5 Minutes

topics.title: Expert Parallelism
topics.description: Expert Parallelism distributes MoE experts across GPUs so each GPU hosts multiple complete experts. Tokens are routed to the GPU holding their activated experts, and each expert runs independently within a single GPU without splitting across multiple. EP has lower inter-GPU communication overhead than Tensor Parallelism and scales well to multi-node deployments via InfiniBand.
resources: Expert Parallelism: Distributing Experts Across Devices

topics.title: Few-Step Image Generation
topics.description: Few-step image generation models produce usable images in eight or fewer denoising steps by training the model to collapse the standard 30 to 50 step process into a fraction of the iterations. Techniques include latent consistency distillation and adversarial training, both of which teach the model to reach high-quality outputs in fewer passes. They are a strong fit for latency-sensitive use cases like real-time filters, but produce noticeably lower quality than full-step models and are a model selection decision rather than an inference optimization technique.
resources: Latent Consistency Models: Synthesizing High-Resolution Images with Few-Step Inference

topics.title: Fine-Tuning
topics.description: Fine-tuning takes a pretrained foundation model and adapts it to a specific domain by training on additional labeled data. A small fine-tuned model can match a much larger general model on constrained tasks like text-to-SQL. Smaller models are faster and cheaper to serve, so fine-tuning is one of the highest-leverage tools for hitting latency and cost targets.
resources: How I Fine-Tuned Granite-Vision 2B to Beat a 90B Model
Is Fine-Tuning Still Needed? LLMs, RAG, & LoRA

topics.title: FlashAttention
topics.description: FlashAttention is a series of hand-optimized CUDA kernels that compute attention with fewer reads and writes to GPU memory by fusing the attention algorithm into a single kernel. Standard attention stores intermediate matrices to memory between steps; FlashAttention eliminates those round-trips. FlashAttention 3 targets Hopper GPUs and FlashAttention 4 targets Blackwell GPUs.
resources: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
Flash Attention: The Fastest Attention Mechanism?
FlashAttention-2: Faster Attention with Better Parallelism and Work Partitioning

topics.title: Frameworks and Libraries
topics.description: Frameworks and libraries sit above CUDA and below inference engines, providing the abstractions that inference engineers interact with most directly. This group covers PyTorch and the Hugging Face ecosystem that supply the model implementations and tooling the rest of the stack depends on.

topics.title: Geo-Aware Load Balancing
topics.description: A global load balancer routes requests to the GPU cluster geographically closest to the requesting user. Network latency accumulates at roughly 5 milliseconds per time zone traversed, so routing a request from Singapore to San Francisco adds 50 to 100 milliseconds of unnecessary overhead. Geo-aware routing ensures that spare capacity in a distant region is used only when nearby capacity is exhausted.
resources: How Geographic Load Balancing Improves Performance

topics.title: GPU Architecture
topics.description: GPU architecture determines the hard limits of what inference can achieve on a given device. This group covers compute, memory, interconnects, and sizing — the four dimensions an inference engineer needs to understand to make informed decisions about hardware selection, parallelism strategy, and optimization priorities.
resources: How do Graphics Cards Work? Exploring GPU Architecture

topics.title: GPU Models
topics.description: Knowing the GPU landscape — which devices are available, what they offer, and how they compare — is practical knowledge for procurement decisions, capacity planning, and understanding which optimizations apply to which hardware. This group covers the NVIDIA architectures that dominate inference deployments and the alternatives worth knowing.
resources: 12 best GPUs for AI and machine learning in 2026
Every 2026 GPU Brand Explained: What’s the Real Difference?

topics.title: GPU Procurement
topics.description: Cloud GPUs are available from hyperscalers like AWS and GCP, GPU-focused neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius, and secondary markets. Procurement mechanisms include reserved instances for predictable baseline load at discounted rates, on-demand instances for flexibility, and spot instances for cost-sensitive batch workloads that tolerate preemption. Large-scale deployments typically combine all three across multiple providers.
resources: Multi-Cloud GPU Strategy: How to Avoid AI Infrastructure Vendor Lock-In
Multi-Cloud GPU Strategy: Definition, Benefits, and Implementation

topics.title: Grace and Vera CPUs
topics.description: NVIDIA's ARM-based Grace and Vera CPUs connect to their paired GPUs via NVLink Chip-to-Chip at up to 900 GB/s, far higher than standard PCIe connections. This high-bandwidth CPU-GPU link makes offloading KV caches and LoRA weights to CPU memory practical, since data can be retrieved quickly enough to remain on the critical path. Grace pairs with Hopper and Blackwell; Vera pairs with the upcoming Rubin architecture.
resources: NVIDIA Vera Rubin: What is it, what's new, and when you can get it

topics.title: Hopper
topics.description: The Hopper architecture, released in 2022 with the H100 and later the H200, introduced FP8 Tensor Cores offering twice the compute throughput of FP16 and asynchronous data transfer features used by FlashAttention 3. H100 and H200 GPUs remain among the most widely deployed inference accelerators due to their maturity, broad software support, and relative availability compared to newer generations.
resources: NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core GPU Architecture
Nvidia Hopper Explained: Why a 2022 GPU Is Still the Smart Money in 2026

topics.title: Image and Video Generation Bottlenecks
topics.description: Image and video generation models are compute-bound because each denoising step applies attention over the entire latent space in parallel, similar to LLM prefill. The models are also relatively small, so memory bandwidth is not the limiting factor. Optimizations focus on FLOPS efficiency rather than memory traffic reduction.
resources: How to Overcome Visual Data Bottlenecks in GenAI Development
6 Limitations of Current AI Video Generation Technology and Workarounds
The biggest bottleneck in AI video generation is not the model, but the cost.
But how do AI images and videos actually work?

topics.title: Image and Video Generation
topics.description: Image and video generation inference is compute-bound rather than memory-bound, making it a different optimization problem from LLM serving. This group covers the production patterns, kernel choices, and parallelism techniques specific to diffusion model deployment.
resources: Understanding AI Image Generation: Models, Tools, and Techniques
Understanding AI Video Generation History: Key Concepts and Impact

topics.title: Image & Video Models
topics.description: Image and video models are specialized artificial intelligence architectures designed to process, interpret, and generate visual data. These models utilize techniques like convolutional neural networks (CNNs), transformers, and diffusion processes to analyze pixel patterns for tasks such as object detection, image classification, and video frame synthesis.
resources: Understanding AI Image Generation: Models, Tools, and Techniques
How do AI models generate videos?
What Are Vision Language Models? How AI Sees & Understands Images
But how do AI images and videos actually work?

topics.title: Image Generation Architecture
topics.description: Image generation models are pipelines of multiple components: a text encoder that converts the prompt into conditioning, a denoising model that iteratively refines a latent representation from noise into an image, and a variational autoencoder that converts the final latent to pixels. The denoising model is the largest and most compute-intensive component and runs up to 100 forward passes per image generation.
resources: How AI Image Generators Work (Stable Diffusion / Dall-E)

topics.title: Image Generation Inference
topics.description: Production image generation inference uses SGLang Diffusion, TensorRT, or hand-optimized PyTorch. The most important optimization target is the attention kernel, where FlashAttention 3 or 4 outperforms the default on Hopper and Blackwell respectively. GEMM kernels for linear layers can be quantized to FP8 safely. Torch compilation with manual kernel plugins caches the compiled engine to avoid multi-minute recompilation on every cold start.
resources: What Is Inference in Generative AI: How It Differs From Traditional Model Inference
Diffusion Models for AI Image Generation
Why Does Diffusion Work Better than Auto-Regression?

topics.title: Independent Component Scaling
topics.description: Multi-model pipelines, like a voice agent that runs VAD, ASR, an LLM, and TTS in sequence, have components with different hardware requirements and traffic patterns. Each component should autoscale independently based on its own load. Running all components within the same Kubernetes cluster minimizes inter-component network latency, which can otherwise consume a significant fraction of a tight latency budget.
resources: Intro to Kubernetes Autoscaling and Best Practices for Implementations

topics.title: Inference Engines
topics.description: Inference engines are the core serving layer that takes model weights and handles requests at production scale. They implement continuous batching, memory management, parallelism, and optimization techniques so engineers do not have to implement these from scratch. This group covers the three dominant LLM engines and the orchestration platform that sits above them.
resources: What is an Inference Engine & Why it’s Essential for Scalable AI
The AI Engineer's Guide to Inference Engines and Frameworks

topics.title: Inference vs. Training
topics.description: Training is the process of learning model weights from data. Inference is serving those weights in production to generate outputs. Training runs are compute-intensive batch jobs; inference is a continuous, latency-sensitive service. Where training success is measured in loss curves, inference success is measured in time to first token, tokens per second, and uptime.

topics.title: Instances and Interconnects
topics.description: Within a node, NVLink connects GPUs one-to-one at up to 1800 GB/s on Blackwell, and NVSwitch creates an all-to-all fabric across all eight GPUs. Between nodes, InfiniBand provides inter-node connectivity at substantially lower bandwidth than NVLink. Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) partitions a single GPU into up to seven isolated slices, each with dedicated compute and memory, allowing small models to run on fractions of a high-end GPU without resource contention.

topics.title: Inter-Token Latency (ITL)
topics.description: ITL is the time between successive generated tokens during decode. An ITL of 10 milliseconds corresponds to 100 tokens per second. It is the per-step measure underlying TPS and is directly tied to how quickly the GPU can complete a single decode forward pass.

topics.title: Inference Engineer
topics.description: Inference engineering is the practice of making generative AI models faster, less expensive, and more reliable to serve in production. It spans the full stack from CUDA kernels and GPU architecture to Kubernetes autoscaling and multi-cloud capacity management. The field emerged alongside the explosion of open models and the shift from pay-per-token APIs to dedicated deployments, where engineers own latency, throughput, cost, and uptime directly.
resources: What Is Inference Engineering? The 2026 GPU Cloud Guide
A Guide to AI Inference Engineering
AI Inference: The Secret to AI's Superpowers

topics.title: Kernel Selection and Fusion
topics.description: A CUDA kernel is a function that runs in parallel across thousands of GPU threads simultaneously. Kernel selection is choosing the best existing kernel for a specific operation; kernel fusion combines sequential kernels into one to eliminate unnecessary reads and writes to VRAM between operations. Libraries like cuBLAS, CUTLASS, CuTe, and FlashInfer provide pre-built kernels for common inference operations, and most inference engines perform kernel selection automatically.
resources: What Is a CUDA Kernel? A Visual Explainer
From Zero to GPU: A Guide to Building and Scaling Production-Ready CUDA Kernels
How to profile CUDA kernels in PyTorch
Master Cuda Programming: Zero to Hero

topics.title: KV Cache Storage
topics.description: KV caches can be stored in GPU VRAM (fastest, tens to hundreds of gigabytes), CPU RAM (slower, hundreds of gigabytes to terabytes), local SSD, or networked SSD. Moving less frequently accessed KV blocks to slower storage frees VRAM for active requests. NVIDIA Dynamo's KV Block Manager provides APIs for managing KV blocks across these storage tiers transparently.
resources: KV Cache Storage Is the New AI Inference Bottleneck
Stop Calling It KV Cache: It’s Something Much Bigger
CacheBlend: Fast Large Language Model Serving for RAG with Cached Knowledge Fusion

topics.title: KV Cache
topics.description: The KV cache stores the key and value tensors computed during attention for each previously processed token. Without it, attention would require recomputing every prior token on each decode step, making inference prohibitively slow. The KV cache lives in GPU memory and its size grows with sequence length and batch size, making it a major target for memory management techniques.
resources: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
KV Caching Explained: Optimizing Transformer Inference Efficiency
How KV Cache Speeds Up LLMs for Faster AI Models on GPUs
The KV Cache: Memory Usage in Transformers

topics.title: Large Language Models
topics.description: An LLM is a decoder-only transformer with three main components: an embedding layer that converts input tokens to vectors, a stack of transformer blocks that process those vectors, and an output language modeling head that converts the final hidden states into a probability distribution over the vocabulary. The configuration file for an open model specifies all architectural details including layer count, hidden dimensions, and attention heads.
resources: Build a Large Language Model From Scratch
What is a Large Language Model (LLM)?

topics.title: Latency Percentiles
topics.description: Mean latency hides outliers. LLM response times follow a right-skewed distribution, so engineers measure P50, P90, P95, and P99. A P99 of several seconds means one in a hundred users has a poor experience even if the median is fast. Reducing P90/P99 latency is as important as reducing average latency.
resources: Percentiles vs averages: why your latency dashboard lies
Latency percentiles for load testing analysis
Mastering Latency Metrics: P90, P95, P99 | System Design

topics.title: Latency vs. Throughput
topics.description: Lower latency means faster responses per user; higher throughput means more total requests served per unit time. These goals are often in tension. Increasing batch size improves throughput but worsens per-user latency. Choosing the right balance is one of the primary decisions in configuring an inference service.
resources: The LLM Inference Trilemma: Throughput, Latency, Cost
LLM inference latency: TTFT, tokens per second, and what to measure
⚖️ Latency vs Throughput: Deep Dive into System Performance Trade‑Offs

topics.title: LLM-based Models
topics.description: LLM-based embedding models use a decoder-only transformer backbone, typically between one and eight billion parameters, to produce higher-quality semantic representations than BERT-style models. They apply a pooling operation to the final layer hidden states and are trained with contrastive objectives on large-scale retrieval datasets. The quality advantage is most pronounced on complex or cross-lingual retrieval tasks; the cost is higher compute per embedding and the need for GPU inference rather than CPU.
resources: LLM Embeddings Explained: A Visual and Intuitive Guide
LLMs are Also Effective Embedding Models: An In-depth Overview
Understanding Embedding Models in the Context of Large Language Models

topics.title: LLM Inference Bottlenecks
topics.description: LLM prefill is compute-bound because it processes the entire input sequence as one large matrix multiplication, performing many operations per byte loaded. LLM decode is memory-bound because it generates tokens one at a time via vector-matrix multiplications that require loading all model weights from memory for each token while performing relatively few arithmetic operations.
resources: Common Bottlenecks in LLM Inference at Scale (And How to Fix Them)
The Hidden Bottlenecks in LLM Inference and How to Fix Them

topics.title: Local and Edge Inference
topics.description: Not all inference runs in a datacenter. Desktop and mobile deployments have different hardware constraints, tooling ecosystems, and use cases from cloud inference. This group covers the patterns and tools for running models on consumer hardware and mobile devices.
resources: AI-Focused Edge Inference: Use Cases And Guide for Enterprise
What Is Local Inference? Definition & Requirements

topics.title: Locust
topics.description: Locust is a general-purpose open-source load testing framework written in Python. In inference benchmarking it is used to simulate realistic user traffic patterns — including request arrival rates, concurrency ramps, and burst scenarios — that synthetic tools do not capture. It is particularly useful for end-to-end load testing that includes network overhead, queuing, and autoscaling behavior rather than raw model server performance alone.
resources: LLM Locust: A Tool for Benchmarking LLM Performance

topics.title: Long Context Handling
topics.description: Long sequences produce KV caches large enough to strain GPU memory, slow down decode, and increase prefill time. Techniques for handling long context include FlashAttention for memory-efficient attention computation, PagedAttention for non-contiguous KV storage, chunked prefill to interleave long prefill with decode, and model-level approaches like sliding window attention that limit how many prior tokens each token attends to.
resources: Ring Attention with Blockwise Transformers for Near-Infinite Context
RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding
What is Long Context and Why Does it Matter for AI?
Long-Context LLM Infrastructure: Building Systems for Million-Token Windows

topics.title: LoRA-Aware Routing
topics.description: LoRA fine-tune weights are small adapter layers loaded on top of a base model to specialize its behavior for a specific task or customer. A deployment serving many LoRA variants for the same base model must route each request to a replica that already has the required LoRA loaded in GPU memory. Routing without this awareness forces constant LoRA swapping, adding latency and reducing throughput on each affected replica.

topics.title: Measuring Quality Impact
topics.description: After quantizing a model, quality must be validated against the original. Three methods are used: perplexity scoring (lower is better, with minimal increase after quantization), standard intelligence benchmarks like MMLU or SWE-bench, and product-specific evals tailored to the actual use case. All three should show differences indistinguishable from noise before a quantized model is deployed.
resources: AI Benchmarks Explained: MMLU, ARC-AGI, and SWE-bench
What do AI Benchmarks Actually Mean?! A Fast Breakdown (MMLU, SWE-bench, & More Explained)

topics.title: Memory
topics.description: GPU memory determines what fits on a single device and how fast data can move through the compute units. VRAM capacity sets the upper limit on model size and KV cache; VRAM bandwidth determines how quickly the decode phase can load weights per token. Modern datacenter GPUs use high-bandwidth memory (HBM) in generations HBM3, HBM3e, and HBM4, stacked directly on the GPU die to maximize bandwidth.
resources: What is GPU Memory and Why it Matters for LLM Inference
NPU vs. CPU vs. GPU vs. TPU: AI Hardware Compared

topics.title: Mixture of Experts (MoE)
topics.description: Mixture of Experts models replace dense linear layers with a set of smaller expert matrices, activating only a subset of experts per token via a learned router. A model like Qwen3-235B activates only 22 billion of its 235 billion parameters per forward pass, making single-user inference efficient. In batched production serving, different tokens activate different experts, so nearly all parameters are active across the batch.
resources: Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer
A Visual Guide to Mixture of Experts (MoE) in LLMs

topics.title: Mobile Inference
topics.description: Mobile devices run inference using vendor frameworks: Google's AI Edge SDK for Android and Apple's Foundation Models and Core ML for iOS. Hardware limitations restrict practical model sizes to one to two billion parameters on current phones. Small fine-tuned models for tasks like transcription, translation, and on-device classification are the strongest fit for mobile edge inference.
resources: Shifting AI inference from the cloud to your phone can reduce AI costs
Cactus: High-Performance AI Inference on Any Smartphone

topics.title: Model Evaluation
topics.description: Model evaluation, or evals, is the practice of systematically measuring model quality for a specific task or domain. Standard intelligence benchmarks like MMLU measure general capabilities but can be gamed; product-specific evals that test real use cases provide more reliable signal. High-confidence evals are a prerequisite before investing in inference optimization, ensuring the model is actually useful before making it fast.
resources: LLM Evaluation Metrics and Methods, Explained Simply
LLM as a Judge: Scaling AI Evaluation Strategies

topics.title: Model Formats and Runtimes
topics.description: Before a model can serve requests, its weights must be stored, loaded, and compiled into an executable form. This group covers the file formats used to distribute weights and the runtimes that compile them into optimized inference engines for specific hardware targets.
resources: Model Weights File Formats in Machine Learning

topics.title: Model Parallelism
topics.description: When a model is too large to fit on a single GPU, or when serving latency requires more compute than one device can provide, model parallelism distributes the workload across multiple GPUs or nodes. This group covers the three parallelism strategies and their trade-offs in terms of communication overhead, latency, and hardware requirements.

topics.title: Model Selection
topics.description: The most important decision in model performance optimization is which model to use. Smaller models with fewer parameters are faster and cheaper to serve than larger ones. The goal is to find the smallest model that meets quality requirements for the task. Model architecture also determines which inference engines and optimization techniques are available, so popular architectures with broad tooling support are preferable.
resources: Beyond Vibes: How to Properly Select the Right LLM for the Right Task
How to Pick the Right AI Foundation Model
How to Choose Large Language Models: A Developer’s Guide to LLMs

topics.title: ModelOpt
topics.description: ModelOpt is NVIDIA's toolkit for post-training quantization, supporting FP8, INT8, FP4, MXFP8, MXFP4, and NVFP4 output formats. It integrates with PyTorch and exports quantized models directly to TensorRT-LLM, vLLM, and SGLang. Calibration runs a small set of representative inputs through the model to compute per-layer scale factors that minimize the gap between quantized and original outputs.
resources: Optimize Models with NVIDIA Model Optimizer
Model Quantization: Post-Training Quantization Using NVIDIA Model Optimizer

topics.title: Multi-Cloud
topics.description: Multi-cloud inference distributes GPU capacity across providers and regions to maximize availability, minimize latency, and meet data residency requirements. This group covers procurement strategy, capacity management, geographic routing, and the reliability patterns that make large-scale inference resilient to hardware and provider failures.
resources: How to Do Agentic AI Inference in a Multicloud, Multi-Model World
Multi-Cloud GPU Strategy: How to Avoid AI Infrastructure Vendor Lock-In
What is Multicloud? How Do You Manage It?

topics.title: Multi-Node Inference
topics.description: Multi-node inference spreads a model across more than eight GPUs using InfiniBand for inter-node communication. It is necessary for the largest models where a single node lacks sufficient VRAM for weights and KV cache. InfiniBand bandwidth is an order of magnitude lower than NVLink, so parallelism strategies must minimize cross-node communication. For MoE models, Expert Parallelism is preferred over Tensor Parallelism between nodes.
resources: How multi-node inference works for massive LLMs like DeepSeek-R1
AI Models Are Huge, but Your GPUs Aren’t: Mastering Multi-Node Distributed Inference

topics.title: N-gram Speculation
topics.description: N-gram speculation builds a dictionary during prefill that maps token prefixes to observed n-gram continuations from the input. During decode, generated tokens are looked up in this dictionary and matching suffixes become draft tokens with no separate model required. It is most effective for code completion, where output frequently mirrors input syntax, and can produce very long draft sequences with high acceptance rates in that domain.
resources: Introducing N-gram Speculative Decoding: Faster Inference for Structured Tasks
What is N-gram Speculation in LLMs and How Does It Speed Up Generation?
Break the Sequential Dependency of LLM Inference Using Lookahead Decoding

topics.title: Neural Networks
topics.description: A neural network is a layered structure of nodes where each node applies a learned weight matrix and bias to its input. Multiple layers connected in sequence form the foundation for all generative AI models. Inference engineers need a working model of how neural networks compute outputs to understand where performance bottlenecks arise.
resources: But what is a neural network?

topics.title: NIMs
topics.description: NIMs are pre-built Docker containers provided by NVIDIA for popular open models, available as flexible multi-LLM containers or as GPU- and model-specific optimized containers. They provide a ready-made starting point for serving common architectures without building a custom container from scratch. For maximum control and custom configurations, starting from a less opinionated base image and building up is generally preferable.
resources: How to Self-Host LLMs and Multi-Modal AI Models with NVIDIA NIM in 5 Minutes

topics.title: NVIDIA Dynamo
topics.description: Dynamo supports conditional disaggregation, where requests are first sent to the decode engine and only routed to a prefill engine when the input is long or not already cached. The ratio of prefill to decode engines is configurable at runtime and can shift as traffic patterns change. This dynamic allocation prevents the prefill queue from becoming a bottleneck and avoids wasting decode engine resources on prefill-heavy traffic.
resources: NVIDIA Dynamo 1.0: Disaggregated LLM Inference Deployment Guide (2026)
NVIDIA Dynamo in 5 Minutes: What Is It and Why Now?

topics.title: NVIDIA Dynamo
topics.description: Dynamo is NVIDIA's open-source distributed serving platform that sits above inference engines and provides orchestration for large-scale deployments. It adds KV-aware routing, disaggregated prefill/decode serving, multi-node parallelism, and an SLA-based planner that dynamically adjusts the number of prefill and decode workers based on TTFT and TPS targets.
resources: Distributed Inference 101: Getting Started with NVIDIA Dynamo
NVIDIA Dynamo in 5 Minutes: What Is It and Why Now?

topics.title: NVIDIA GenAI-Perf
topics.description: GenAI-Perf is NVIDIA's inference benchmarking tool, designed to work across TensorRT-LLM, Triton Inference Server, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints. It generates synthetic workloads with configurable sequence length distributions and concurrency levels and outputs standard latency and throughput metrics including TTFT, ITL, and TPS percentiles.

topics.title: NVIDIA
topics.description: NVIDIA GPUs are the dominant hardware for inference due to their combination of Tensor Core compute, HBM bandwidth, NVLink interconnects, and the CUDA software ecosystem. The three most relevant architectures for current inference deployments are Hopper, Blackwell, and the Grace and Vera CPU platforms that pair with them.
resources: Top 12 NVIDIA GPUs for AI Training & Inference in 2026
Every Nvidia Graphics Card Explained as Simply as Possible

topics.title: Observability
topics.description: Inference observability tracks total request volume, input and output sequence lengths, response codes, latency percentiles (P50, P90, P99 of TTFT, TPS, and end-to-end latency), replica count, GPU utilization, and queue depth. These metrics are interdependent; a latency spike could come from long input sequences, high concurrency, or a hardware issue. Observability must integrate with existing tooling like Grafana, Datadog, and PagerDuty to put inference metrics in context.
resources: LLM Observability: A Complete Guide to Monitoring Production Deployments
What is LLM Observability? The Ultimate Guide for AI Developers

topics.title: Omni-Modal Models
topics.description: Omni models accept multiple input modalities and produce multiple output types in a single model. They avoid the latency of running separate specialized models in sequence but often lag behind dedicated models in quality within each modality. Production pipelines using VLMs typically coordinate preprocessing steps like OCR, audio transcription, and PDF extraction as separate independently scaling components.
resources: OmniModels: The Unified Architecture for Intelligence

topics.title: Online vs. Offline Inference
topics.description: Online inference serves real-time user-facing requests where latency matters. Offline inference processes large batches of data asynchronously where throughput and cost matter more than per-request speed. The same model, like Whisper for transcription, may need separate deployments for each use case because the optimal configurations differ significantly.
resources: Production ML systems: Static versus dynamic inference
Trade-offs in Online vs Offline Model Inference
Offline Recurrence for Improved Online Inference

topics.title: ONNX Runtime
topics.description: ONNX Runtime is an open-source inference runtime that executes models exported to the ONNX format, which stores both weights and a computation graph for cross-platform portability. It supports multiple hardware backends including CUDA, DirectML, and CPU. It is widely used for embedding models, vision models, and pipelines that need to run across hardware environments without engine-specific configuration.
resources: ONNX – open format for machine learning models​

topics.title: Open vs. Closed Models
topics.description: Closed models are accessed exclusively through a vendor API; the weights are never released. Open models publish their weights for download and self-hosting. For inference engineers, this distinction determines the entire problem space: closed models require no infrastructure but offer no control over latency, cost, or configuration, while open models require building and operating a full inference stack but give complete control over every layer of it.
resources: AI Engineering: Building Applications with Foundation Models
Open-source Models vs. Closed-Source Models: A Simple Guide
Open-Source vs. Closed LLMs: A Guide
Open Source vs Closed AI: LLMs, Agents & the AI Stack Explained

topics.title: Ops:Byte Ratio
topics.description: The ops:byte ratio is a property of GPU hardware that expresses the balance between compute throughput and memory bandwidth. It is calculated by dividing peak FLOPS by peak memory bandwidth, and sets the threshold that separates compute-bound from memory-bound workloads on that device. Different GPU generations have very different ops:byte ratios, which is why an optimization that works well on one generation may have no effect on another.
resources: A guide to LLM inference and performance

topics.title: Other Accelerators
topics.description: Alternatives to NVIDIA GPUs include AMD MI350, Google TPUs, AWS Inferentia and Trainium, Cerebras WSE-3, and Groq LPUs. Each offers a specific advantage: AMD provides CUDA-compatible tooling via ROCm; TPUs integrate deeply with Google Cloud and JAX; Inferentia and Trainium offer cost advantages within AWS. All face the shared challenge of building an ecosystem to match the breadth of NVIDIA's CUDA libraries and inference engine support.
resources: Top 12 Cloud GPU Providers for AI and Machine Learning in 2026
Every 2026 GPU Brand Explained: What’s the Real Difference?

topics.title: PagedAttention
topics.description: PagedAttention stores the KV cache in fixed-size pages rather than a single contiguous memory block, allowing it to be distributed across GPU memory without fragmentation. It uses a lookup table to access pages on demand, reducing memory waste from over-allocation and enabling more requests to share GPU memory. It is the memory management technique that made vLLM's high throughput possible.
resources: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention

topics.title: Performance Benchmarking
topics.description: Benchmarking measures inference service performance under realistic workloads. Good benchmarks simulate realistic input and output sequence lengths, concurrency patterns, and request contents rather than synthetic uniform inputs. Standard tools include SGLang Genai-bench, NVIDIA GenAI-Perf, and Locust. Always establish a baseline before applying optimizations and change one variable at a time.

topics.title: Pipeline Parallelism
topics.description: Pipeline Parallelism splits an LLM's layers into sequential stages and assigns each stage to a different GPU or node. Unlike Tensor Parallelism, each GPU holds complete layers rather than layer fragments. It introduces pipeline bubbles where GPUs wait for preceding stages, reducing efficiency. It is used for multi-node inference with dense models, typically combined with Tensor Parallelism within each node.
resources: LLM Training — Fundamentals of Pipeline Parallelism
What Is Pipeline Parallelism and How to Use It

topics.title: Post-Training Quantization
topics.description: Post-training quantization converts finished model weights to lower precision after training is complete, using a small calibration dataset to compute per-layer scale factors that minimize the gap between quantized and original outputs. It is the standard approach for most deployments since it requires no retraining and can be applied to any existing model. The leading tool is NVIDIA ModelOpt, which exports quantized models in formats compatible with all major inference engines.
resources: AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration
Optimizing LLMs for Performance and Accuracy with Post-Training Quantization

topics.title: Prefill and Decode Phases
topics.description: LLM inference has two distinct phases. Prefill processes the entire input sequence in parallel to build the KV cache and is compute-bound. Decode generates output tokens one at a time by reading model weights from memory and is memory-bound. Each phase has different bottlenecks and responds to different optimization techniques.
resources: Prefill vs Decode: LLM Inference Phases Explained
Understanding the Two Key Stages of LLM Inference: Prefill and Decode(Part-1)
Why LLMs Read Fast but Write Slowly - Prefill vs Decode

topics.title: Profiling Performance
topics.description: Profiling reveals where time is spent within a benchmark, identifying which operations consume the most compute or memory. Tools include PyTorch Profiler, NVIDIA Nsight Systems for system-wide GPU and CPU analysis, and NVIDIA Nsight Compute for per-kernel analysis. Profiling is most useful when writing custom inference code or contributing to inference frameworks, rather than configuring existing engines.

topics.title: PyTorch
topics.description: PyTorch is the standard Python framework for building and running neural networks. It abstracts CUDA into a tensor operation API and provides automatic differentiation for training. For inference, PyTorch supports torch.compile for automatic kernel optimization and serves as the foundation that all major inference engines build on top of.
resources: Creating a conda Environment for Pytorch and Cuda
How to profile CUDA kernels in PyTorch

topics.title: Quantization-Aware Training
topics.description: Quantization-aware training computes scale factors and optimizes model weights jointly during training so the final model is already calibrated for the target low-precision format. This produces better quality at low precision than post-training quantization but requires retraining the model from scratch or from a checkpoint. Some labs release models trained this way, such as GPT-OSS in MXFP4.
resources: How Quantization Aware Training Enables Low-Precision Accuracy Recovery
Quantization Aware Training (QAT) With a Custom DataLoader

topics.title: Quantization
topics.description: Quantization converts model weights and other values from their native precision to a lower-precision format. Cutting precision in half doubles memory bandwidth for decode and enables twice the FLOPS for prefill on compatible Tensor Cores. The tradeoff is potential quality loss from reduced numerical precision, which can compound across the many calculations in a forward pass.
resources: AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration
How LLMs survive in low precision | Quantization Fundamentals

topics.title: Real-Time Factor (RTF)
topics.description: RTF measures how quickly an ASR system can process audio relative to its duration. A system that transcribes one hour of audio in six seconds has an RTF of 600x. It is the standard throughput metric for long-file transcription workloads and improves roughly linearly with the number of GPUs used for parallel chunk processing.
resources: What is RTF (Real-Time Factor) in ASR?    Copied from: https://www.futurebeeai.com/knowledge-hub/real-time-factor-asr

topics.title: Reasoning Models
topics.description: Reasoning models generate an intermediate thinking sequence before producing their final output, adding a third token sequence alongside the input and output. This reasoning trace increases total token count significantly and changes inference economics: TTFT is higher, total latency is longer, and output token costs dominate. Inference engineers must account for the variable and sometimes very long reasoning sequences when sizing infrastructure and setting latency budgets.
resources: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
What Are Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)? Smarter AI Beyond LLMs
How do thinking and reasoning models work?

topics.title: Request Queueing
topics.description: A request queue holds incoming traffic when all active replicas are at capacity while autoscaling brings new replicas online. A first-in, first-out queue is the standard implementation; priority queues can give paid users better position. Queues must be visible to newly started replicas so that requests are not held waiting for existing replicas when new capacity becomes available.
resources: Efficient Request Queueing – Optimizing LLM Performance
Why Do AI Requests Queue? | Inside vLLM

topics.title: Roofline Model
topics.description: The roofline model is a visual framework for reasoning about hardware performance limits. It plots arithmetic intensity on the x-axis against achievable performance on the y-axis, with two ceilings: a diagonal memory bandwidth ceiling for low-intensity workloads and a horizontal compute ceiling for high-intensity ones. A workload's position relative to these ceilings shows not just whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound, but how far it sits from the hardware's theoretical maximum — which tells you how much headroom remains before an optimization hits a hard limit.
resources: A very short intro to the Roofline model

topics.title: Routing and Load Balancing
topics.description: Routers make request-level decisions about which replica to send a request to, considering factors like KV cache prefix match and LoRA availability. Load balancers make system-level decisions to distribute traffic evenly across replicas. In systems with prefix caching, naive round-robin load balancing misses cache opportunities; intelligent routing increases cache hit rates and reduces TTFT.
resources: LLM Inference Serving: Architecture, Routing & Auto-Scaling
LLM Model Routing: Route Queries to the Right Model Automatically
LLM Load Balancing: Concepts, Strategies & Best Practices

topics.title: Safetensors
topics.description: Safetensors is the standard format for storing and distributing open model weights. It uses memory mapping for fast, zero-copy loading and prevents execution of arbitrary code during deserialization, making it safer than earlier pickle-based formats. All major inference engines load safetensors natively, and most open models on Hugging Face publish weights in this format.
resources: SafeTensors: Efficient Serialization Format for Deep Learning
Hugging Face SafeTensors LLMs in Ollama

topics.title: Scale to Zero
topics.description: Scale to zero allows the system to run zero replicas during periods of no traffic and spin up on demand. It requires fast cold starts and robust queuing to hold incoming requests while a replica starts. Scale to zero is well-suited for development environments and periodically accessed workloads, but not for latency-sensitive production applications with unpredictable light traffic.
resources: Should LLM Serving Scale to Zero for Cost
Runpod Secrets: Scaling LLM Inference to Zero Cost During Downtime
Zero Redundancy Optimizer (ZeRO): Scaling LLM Training Without Breaking the Bank

topics.title: Security and Compliance
topics.description: Inference infrastructure must protect user inputs, model outputs, and model weights. Standard practices include data encryption, container security, network isolation, and access controls validated by third-party penetration testing. Regulated industries require compliance with frameworks like SOC 2 and HIPAA, which also apply to underlying cloud providers. Multi-cloud deployments support data residency requirements by routing each country's data to clusters in that country.
resources: Inference security: How to protect APIs in production AI systems
How to achieve compliance and security in AI inference
Are your AI Inference and GenAI Environments Secure? These Five Essentials Will Help

topics.title: SGLang Genai-bench
topics.description: SGLang Genai-bench is a benchmarking tool built into the SGLang project for measuring LLM inference throughput and latency under realistic request distributions. It supports variable input and output sequence lengths and concurrent request patterns, making it well-suited for validating SGLang and vLLM deployments before production.

topics.title: SGLang
topics.description: SGLang is a high-throughput inference engine with a flexible frontend language for customizing server behavior. It has strong support for MoE models like DeepSeek and Qwen and works closely with model labs to optimize new architectural features. SGLang Diffusion extends it to image and video generation models with pipeline abstractions and diffusion-specific parallelism.
resources: SGLang vs vLLM: Which LLM Inference Framework Should You Use?

topics.title: Shared vs. Dedicated Inference
topics.description: Shared inference means sending requests to a public API and paying per token. Dedicated inference means renting GPUs and running your own model server, paying per GPU-hour. Shared inference is simpler and has no cold start, but dedicated inference offers control over latency, cost at scale, model customization, and uptime. Most products start shared and move to dedicated as traffic grows.
resources: Dedicated vs shared LLM inference: when reserved capacity makes sense
Self-Hosted LLM: A Practical Guide for DevOps
When shared inference is not enough: the case for dedicated AI endpoints

topics.title: Sizing and Procurement
topics.description: Estimating GPU requirements starts with VRAM: roughly 1 GB per billion parameters at FP8 for weights, plus at least 50 percent headroom for the KV cache. This total is rounded up to the nearest available instance size. Cloud GPUs are available from hyperscalers like AWS and GCP, neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius, and spot markets; large deployments combine reserved instances for baseline load with on-demand and spot capacity for bursts.
resources: GPU Requirements for LLM Inference: Memory, Throughput, and Sizing
Inference Is the New Bottleneck: How to Plan GPU Capacity for Production AI

topics.title: Speculative Decoding
topics.description: Speculative decoding takes advantage of spare compute during memory-bound decode by generating multiple draft tokens and validating them in a single forward pass. If the target model accepts N draft tokens, the forward pass produces N+1 tokens instead of one. The performance gain depends on draft token cost, draft sequence length, and acceptance rate, which decreases at higher temperatures and larger batch sizes.
resources: An Introduction to Speculative Decoding for Reducing Latency in AI Inference
Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding
Faster LLMs: Accelerate Inference with Speculative Decoding
Speculative Decoding: When Two LLMs are Faster than One

topics.title: Speech-to-Speech Models
topics.description: Speech-to-speech models unify ASR, reasoning, and TTS into a single model by expanding the LLM vocabulary with audio input and output tokens, eliminating the latency of cascading three separate models in sequence. Current closed models like OpenAI's gpt-4o-realtime exist but remain more expensive and less capable than well-tuned cascading pipelines of dedicated ASR, LLM, and TTS models. Open speech-to-speech models are an active research area without commercially viable options at the time of writing.
resources: What Is Speech-to-Speech? Uses, Benefits & How It Works
Speech-to-Speech Model Research at Google DeepMind

topics.title: Speech
topics.description: Speech inference covers the pipeline from raw audio to text and back, including the detection, transcription, diarization, and synthesis steps that make up voice applications. Each component has distinct inference characteristics and often runs on separate hardware to avoid resource contention.
resources: How streaming ASR inference differs from LLM serving
Speech LLMs: Models that listen and talk back

topics.title: Streaming and Protocol Support
topics.description: Text streaming over HTTP is sufficient for LLM chat applications. For real-time voice and video applications, WebSockets provide a persistent bidirectional connection for continuous unstructured data like audio chunks. gRPC provides bidirectional streaming for structured service-to-service communication with schema enforcement. Each WebSocket connection holds a slot on the server, and the concurrency limit must be set to match the GPU's sustainable load.
resources: AI for Web Devs: Faster Responses with HTTP Streaming

topics.title: Streaming TTS
topics.description: Real-time TTS streams audio continuously over WebSockets rather than returning a complete file after generation finishes. The audio decoder converts token streams to waveforms as they are generated, implemented in compiled PyTorch with dynamic batching. After tuning the inference engine and decoder, the primary performance lever is how many concurrent real-time streams a single GPU replica can sustain.
resources: Streaming Speech to Text Models - Kyutai vs Whisper

topics.title: Structured Outputs
topics.description: Structured outputs constrain model generation to a defined schema — typically JSON, a specific data type, or a function signature — so that downstream code can parse the result directly without a repair pass. Major inference engines including vLLM and SGLang ship structured output as a first-class feature. The tradeoff is that a schema guarantees the shape of the output, not its correctness: if the model's best answer does not naturally conform to the schema, forcing conformance can affect response quality.
resources: Structured Output Engineering for Production LLMs: Beyond JSON Mode

topics.title: Tensor Parallelism
topics.description: Tensor Parallelism splits each layer's weight matrices across multiple GPUs and distributes the matmul computation. Each GPU handles a shard of each layer and the results are combined via an all-reduce operation before the next layer. It reduces per-user latency by sharing both VRAM and compute across GPUs, but requires fast NVLink interconnects and is not well-suited for multi-node deployments.
resources: What Is Tensor Parallelism and How to Apply It

topics.title: TensorRT-LLM
topics.description: TensorRT-LLM is NVIDIA's inference engine combining PyTorch-based model execution with proprietary NVIDIA kernels unavailable in other engines. It achieves the highest performance among the three major engines, with excellent support for Hopper and Blackwell architectures and NVIDIA-specific formats like NVFP4. The tradeoff is a steeper learning curve and narrower model support compared to vLLM or SGLang.
resources: TensorRT LLM 1.0 Livestream: New Easy-To-Use Pythonic Runtime

topics.title: TensorRT
topics.description: TensorRT is NVIDIA's high-performance inference runtime that compiles PyTorch or ONNX models into optimized engines using fused kernels, quantization, and hardware-specific tuning. It is the standard choice for image and video generation models and for any workload where maximum throughput on NVIDIA hardware is the primary goal. Compiled engines are cached to disk, eliminating recompilation overhead on subsequent cold starts.

topics.title: Testing and Deployment
topics.description: Deploying inference services safely requires tools for rolling out changes without downtime, estimating costs before committing to a configuration, and maintaining visibility into system health once live. This group covers the deployment, cost, observability, and compliance concerns that apply once a service is ready for production traffic.

topics.title: Text-to-Speech (TTS)
topics.description: Modern TTS models like Orpheus TTS are fine-tuned LLMs with an expanded vocabulary that includes audio tokens. They generate audio token sequences decoded to waveforms by a small audio decoder. The key performance metrics are time to first byte of audio (TTFB) and the number of concurrent real-time streams a single GPU replica can sustain, rather than raw token throughput.
resources: Create your own voices with Gemini 3.8 text-to-speech

topics.title: The Inference Stack
topics.description: A complete inference system has three layers: runtime, infrastructure, and tooling. The runtime layer optimizes a single model on a single instance using techniques like batching, caching, quantization, and speculation. The infrastructure layer scales across clusters, regions, and cloud providers while maintaining uptime. The tooling layer provides the right level of abstraction for engineers to control the system productively. All three must work together for mission-critical inference at scale.

topics.title: Time to First Token (TTFT)
topics.description: TTFT measures how long it takes for a user to receive the first output token after submitting a request. It is determined primarily by the prefill phase and by queue time. For streaming applications like chatbots, TTFT is the most visible latency signal and directly affects perceived responsiveness.
resources: What is time to first token (TTFT)?
What Is Time to First Token?
Most devs don't understand how LLM tokens work

topics.title: Tokens Per Second (TPS)
topics.description: TPS measures how many tokens are delivered to the user per second after the first token. It is determined by the decode phase and reflects memory bandwidth efficiency. Per-user TPS (also called perceived TPS) is a latency metric; total TPS across the inference service is a throughput metric.
resources: LLM Speed Tiers Explained: What TPS (Token Per Second) Actually Feels Like

topics.title: Transformer Blocks
topics.description: Transformer blocks are the repeated hidden layers of an LLM. Each block contains an attention sublayer, a feed-forward neural network sublayer, and normalization layers. The feed-forward network holds the majority of model parameters, while attention is the most computationally complex operation per token.
resources: What Are Transformer Models and How Do They Work?
A Simplified Explanation of the Transformer Block

topics.title: Hugging Face Transformers and Diffusers
topics.description: The transformers and diffusers libraries provide reference implementations of popular LLM and image/video generation architectures. They are not designed for production serving but are essential for understanding model configurations, downloading weights, and prototyping inference. Model cards on Hugging Face use transformers or diffusers sample code as the canonical usage examples.
resources: Getting Started With Hugging Face in 15 Minutes

topics.title: Video Generation Inference
topics.description: Video generation models run on full nodes of eight GPUs with a batch size of one because the latent space is too large to batch effectively. Attention over the three-dimensional video latent space consumes 70 to 80 percent of compute time and is the primary optimization target. Attention caching techniques that reuse outputs from previous timesteps or transformer layers can improve speed by 30 to 40 percent.
resources: TeaCache: Timestep Embedding Tells: It's Time to Cache for Video Diffusion Model
How do AI video generation models work?

topics.title: Video Generation Models
topics.description: Video generation models extend image generation to three-dimensional latent space, representing width, height, and time simultaneously. They run the same number of denoising steps as image models but process far more data per step. Attention over the full video latent space dominates compute time, making video generation the most resource-intensive common inference workload.
resources: How do AI models generate videos?
How do AI video generation models work?

topics.title: Video Processing for VLMs
topics.description: One second of video contains 24 frames, each requiring roughly 1,000 tokens to represent at full resolution. This makes video inputs extremely long-context workloads. Frame rate reduction and downsampling are practically mandatory for running video through a VLM in a single request. Prefix caching and chunked prefill become critical for managing the resulting multi-thousand-token sequences.
resources: Vision Language Model Prompt Engineering Guide for Image and Video Understanding
Exploring the Limits of VLMs: A Dataset for Evaluating Text-to-Video Generation

topics.title: Vision Language Models (VLMs)
topics.description: VLMs combine a large language model with a small vision encoder that converts input images or video into a sequence of visual tokens. A high-resolution image typically adds about 1,000 tokens to the input sequence. All LLM inference optimization techniques apply to VLMs, but longer sequences make quantization, prefix caching, and disaggregation especially important.
resources: A Multimodal World - Hugging Face Computer Vision Course
What Are Vision Language Models? How AI Sees & Understands Images

topics.title: vLLM
topics.description: vLLM is the most widely adopted LLM inference engine, offering broad support for model architectures, hardware platforms (NVIDIA, AMD, Google TPUs), and optimization techniques including prefix caching, quantization, speculative decoding, and parallelism. Its primary advantage is ease of adoption and the fastest day-zero support for newly released open models. It also supports multimodal inference via vLLM Omni.
resources: What is vLLM? Efficient AI Inference for Large Language Models

topics.title: Voice Activity Detection (VAD)
topics.description: VAD is a lightweight model that monitors an audio stream or file and identifies segments containing speech, filtering out silence. It is a required preprocessing component in both real-time ASR pipelines and long-file transcription pipelines, splitting audio into discrete chunks at natural speech boundaries rather than fixed time intervals. VAD runs on dedicated hardware to avoid competing with the ASR model for GPU resources.
resources: Voice Activity Detection (VAD): The Complete 2026 Guide to Speech Detection
Voice Activity Detection | The key to realtime voice chat

topics.title: Writing Custom Kernels
topics.description: Custom kernels are written when existing libraries do not fully utilize a GPU's capabilities for a specific operation or architecture. Most production kernels are written in C++ using CUTLASS and CuTe for GEMM-style operations and FlashInfer for attention variants; Triton offers a Python-based alternative with a lower barrier to entry. Writing an effective kernel requires understanding the target GPU's memory hierarchy, SM occupancy, and Tensor Core instruction set — skills that sit at the intersection of software and hardware.
resources: CUDA by Example: An Introduction to General-Purpose GPU Programming

topics.title: Zero-Downtime Deployment
topics.description: Canary deployments update inference services without interrupting live traffic by routing a small percentage of requests to the new deployment, monitoring for issues, and gradually shifting traffic over. Blue-green deployments, which cut all traffic at once to a parallel environment, are impractical for large inference workloads because they require doubling GPU capacity during the transition. With autoscaling, canary deployments are low cost since the old service scales down as the new one takes traffic.
resources: Zero-Downtime Deployments: A Practical Guide for Busy Engineers
How do software systems achieve zero downtime on new deploys?
Zero Downtime Deployments in Kubernetes Explained
